title: Given an array of positive numbers and a target sum, find the length of the smallest contiguous subarray whose sum is greater than or equal to the target. If no such subarray exists, return zero. (LeetCode: Minimum Size Subarray Sum)
shortTitle: Smallest Subarray with a Given Sum (Variable-Size Sliding Window)
keyPoints: Grow the window on the right until the sum reaches the target, then shrink from the left as far as possible.
The technique works because all numbers are positive: adding increases the sum, removing decreases it.
Each pointer only moves forward, so total work is O(n) despite the inner shrink loop.
Return zero if no window ever reaches the target to signal the no-solution case.
With negative numbers, this approach breaks; use prefix sums with a monotonic deque instead.
This is the variable-size sliding window, distinct from the fixed-size version where the window width is constant.

s1_definition.oneliner: Grow right until you hit the target, then shrink left as far as you can, tracking the smallest length.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Variable-size sliding window** – the window grows and shrinks dynamically based on a running-sum condition.
- **Expand** – move the right pointer forward, adding each element to the running sum.
- **Shrink** – when the sum reaches the target, move the left pointer forward while the sum still meets the target, recording the smallest window length.
- **Positivity requirement** – all numbers must be positive for the grow/shrink logic to be valid.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time, O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh needs to collect at least a target rupee amount from a run of consecutive daily deposits using the shortest possible stretch of days. He grows his stretch by adding the next day on the right until the total reaches the target, then trims days off the left as long as the total still meets the target, noting how short the stretch got.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The smallest-subarray-with-a-given-sum problem is the variable-size sliding window. The key difference from the fixed-size version is that the window grows and shrinks dynamically based on a condition rather than staying a constant width.

You keep a running sum, a left pointer, and a best length initialized to infinity. You expand the right pointer, adding each element. The moment the sum reaches or exceeds the target, you have a qualifying window, so you record its length and shrink from the left as much as possible while the sum still meets the target. That inner shrink finds the shortest qualifying window ending at the current right position.

At the National Bank of India, the treasury team wanted to raise at least a target amount of liquidity from a run of consecutive daily deposits using the shortest possible stretch. Because daily deposits are all positive, the grow-and-shrink window gave the shortest qualifying stretch in a single linear pass.

The O(n) guarantee comes from the amortized analysis: each element is added once and removed at most once, so total pointer movements are at most 2n. The positivity of all numbers is essential; with negatives, adding an element could decrease the sum and the shrink logic would break.

Remember one sentence: grow the window right until the sum reaches the target, then shrink the window left as far as possible, and the smallest window seen is the answer.
